_comment: Plaintext source for per-clue structured analysis. Author here in plain English, then run `node scripts/apply-minute-cryptic-analysis.mjs` to base64-encode and merge into puzzles.json. Keyed by puzzle id.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Warning" at the start of the clue. The answer ALERT is a noun meaning a warning or signal to stay watchful.
analyses.device: This is an anagram. The indicator is "mixed" — it tells you to rearrange the letters of the fodder word LATER.
steps: Take the fodder: LATER (5 letters: L, A, T, E, R).
"mixed" signals an anagram, so reorder those five letters.
analyses.note: Don't be thrown by "oddly": it colours the surface reading ("oddly mixed") but isn't a second instruction. The one operative signal is "mixed", and the letter count (5) matches LATER exactly — a quick check that you have the right fodder.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Quiet". SILENT means making or having no sound.
analyses.device: This is an anagram, signalled by "mixed". The fodder is LISTEN, which has the same six letters as the answer.
steps: Take the fodder: LISTEN (L, I, S, T, E, N).
"mixed" tells you to rearrange those six letters.
analyses.note: LISTEN and SILENT are a classic anagram pair — same letters, opposite ideas. Spotting a six-letter word sitting in the clue beside an anagram word like "mixed" is your cue to test it as fodder.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Plot" — a garden plot, a patch of cultivated ground.
analyses.device: This is an anagram of DANGER. The indicator is "turned around", here meaning the letters are shuffled.
steps: Take the fodder: DANGER (D, A, N, G, E, R).
analyses.note: "turned around" can look like a reversal cue, but DANGER reversed is REGNAD — not a word. The letters instead rearrange to GARDEN, so treat "turned around" as an anagram signal here.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Paid back" at the front. REPAID means paid back or reimbursed.
analyses.device: This is an anagram. The indicator is "altered", which tells you to rearrange the fodder DIAPER.
steps: Take the fodder: DIAPER (6 letters: D, I, A, P, E, R).
"altered" signals an anagram of those letters.
analyses.note: "after ... is altered" reads smoothly as a sentence, but only "altered" does cryptic work — "after" is surface glue. Confirm the fodder by length: DIAPER and REPAID are both six letters drawn from the same set.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Step". To TREAD is to step or walk.
analyses.device: This is a charade — you build the answer from parts placed in sequence. "with T in front" tells you where one part goes.
steps: Start with the word given in the clue: READ.
"T in front" places the letter T before it.
T + READ joins to spell TREAD.
analyses.note: Charade clues assemble pieces in reading order. "in front" is a position marker — it fixes T at the start rather than the end, which is what separates TREAD from a wrong build like READT.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Sketch". An OUTLINE is a rough sketch or summary.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The clue hands you the two parts directly: OUT + LINE.
steps: OUT + LINE runs together as OUTLINE (3 + 4 = 7).
analyses.note: When a clue spells out "X + Y", the charade is doing the joining for you. The only checks left are order (OUT before LINE) and that the total length matches the (7) enumeration.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Core" — the central or most important part. HEART carries that sense.
analyses.device: This is an anagram, flagged by "scrambled". The fodder is EARTH.
steps: Take the fodder: EARTH (E, A, R, T, H).
"scrambled" tells you to rearrange the five letters.
analyses.note: EARTH and HEART share all five letters. "Core" defines by meaning, not by spelling — so look past the literal earth/heart link and trust the anagram mechanics.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Respond". To REACT is to respond to something.
analyses.device: This is an anagram. The indicator "mixed" acts on the fodder CRATE.
steps: Take the fodder: CRATE (C, R, A, T, E).
analyses.note: CRATE, REACT, CATER and TRACE are all anagrams of one another. When several common words share a letter set, the definition ("Respond") is what pins down which one is wanted.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Dark period". NIGHT is the dark part of the day.
analyses.device: This is an anagram of THING, signalled by "twisted".
steps: Take the fodder: THING (T, H, I, N, G).
"twisted" tells you to rearrange the five letters.
analyses.note: The colon after "Dark period" cleanly separates the definition from the wordplay — a common layout. Everything before it defines; everything after it (THING twisted) builds.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Extra item". A SPARE is something kept in reserve.
analyses.device: This is an anagram. The indicator is "mixed" and the fodder is SPEAR.
steps: Take the fodder: SPEAR (S, P, E, A, R).
analyses.note: SPEAR and SPARE differ only by swapping two letters, so the anagram is gentle. The length (5) and the shared letters confirm you have the right fodder before you commit.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Post". AIRMAIL is post carried by aircraft.
analyses.device: This is a charade with the parts given outright: AIR + MAIL.
analyses.note: "Post" and "AIR + MAIL" both circle the same idea, which makes the surface read naturally. Trust the "+": it is telling you exactly how the answer is assembled.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Evening close". SUNSET is the close of the day.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The clue supplies the parts: SUN + SET.
analyses.note: Both pieces relate to the surface meaning (the sun setting), which is good clue craft. The cryptic work is simply joining the two named words in order.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Night-bright". Something MOONLIT is lit by the moon — bright at night.
analyses.device: This is a charade, and the clue spells the recipe out: MOON + LIT, joined in order.
steps: Take the first part: MOON (4 letters).
Add the second part: LIT (3 letters).
MOON + LIT runs together as MOONLIT (4 + 3 = 7).
analyses.note: When a clue hands you the parts with a literal "+", the charade does the assembling for you. The only check is order and length — MOON before LIT, totalling the seven letters the enumeration promises.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Free leaflet". A HANDOUT is something given away, like a leaflet.
analyses.device: This is a charade built from the stated parts: HAND + OUT.
analyses.note: Note how "hand out" as a phrase already means to distribute — the surface and the wordplay point the same way, which is why charades like this read so smoothly.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Outer garment". An OVERCOAT is a coat worn over other clothes.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The two parts are given: OVER + COAT.
analyses.note: The parts even describe the thing — a coat worn over you. When a charade's pieces double as a near-definition, the (8) enumeration is your final confirmation.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Border". A FRAME is the border around a picture or window.
analyses.device: This is a container clue. The indicator "holding" means one piece wraps around another — FAME holds the letter R.
steps: Insert R after the F: F + R + AME spells FRAME.
analyses.note: With container clues the work is finding where the inner letter lands. "holding" tells you R is enclosed, and testing the gap after the first letter gives the only reading that makes a real word — FRAME.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Small wood". A GROVE is a small group of trees.
analyses.device: This is a container/insertion clue. "ROVE holding G" places the letter G with the word ROVE.
steps: Add G as the clue directs ("holding G").
G leads ROVE to spell GROVE (1 + 4 = 5).
analyses.note: Here the inserted G settles at the front, so the build reads G + ROVE. Always test the candidate against the (5) enumeration and the definition "small wood" to confirm the placement.

analyses.definition: Both halves are definitions. "Leap" defines SPRING (to spring is to leap) and "season" defines SPRING (the time of year).
analyses.device: This is a double definition — there is no wordplay to unpick. The word "and" simply links two separate meanings of the same answer.
steps: Read "Leap" as a definition: SPRING means to jump.
Read "season" as a definition: SPRING is a season.
One six-letter word satisfies both — SPRING.
analyses.note: Double definitions feel odd at first because nothing is spelled out letter by letter. The trick is to find a single word that wears two hats; the (6) enumeration confirms the fit.

analyses.definition: Two definitions point to one word: "Throw" (to pitch a ball) and "musical tone" (the pitch of a note).
analyses.device: This is a double definition. There is no anagram or hidden trick — just two meanings of PITCH side by side.
steps: Read "Throw": to PITCH is to throw.
Read "musical tone": PITCH is how high or low a note sounds.
analyses.note: "or" between the two senses is a typical double-definition link. When neither half looks like wordplay, ask which single word can mean both — that is the whole puzzle.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Intelligent" and "piercing". Both describe SHARP.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. SHARP means clever (intelligent) and also keen-edged or piercing.
steps: Read "Intelligent": a SHARP mind is a clever one.
analyses.note: Adjective double definitions are common — look for a word with both a figurative sense (clever) and a literal one (keen-edged). The (5) length narrows the field.

analyses.definition: The definition is "farm building". A BARN is a farm building.
analyses.device: This is an insertion clue. "Ban with R inserted" puts the letter R inside the word BAN.
steps: B + AR + N — that is, BA(R)N — spells BARN (4).
analyses.note: "inserted" is the container signal. The only question is where R goes; slotting it before the final N gives the one real word, BARN.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Aircraft". A PLANE is an aircraft.
analyses.device: This is a container clue. "PANE containing L" puts the letter L inside PANE.
steps: Place L after the P: P(L)ANE spells PLANE (5).
analyses.note: "containing" marks PANE as the shell and L as the filling. Test the insertion point against the (5) enumeration — only L after the first letter yields a word.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Snare". A TRAP is a snare for catching animals.
analyses.device: This is a container clue. "TAP around R" wraps the word TAP around the letter R.
analyses.note: "around" is the container indicator pointing the other way: TAP is on the outside, R on the inside. Either phrasing ("holding", "around", "containing") means the same enclosure.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Defeat". To BEAT someone is to defeat them.
analyses.device: This is a container clue. "BAT holding E" places the letter E inside BAT.
analyses.note: Short container clues hinge on a single insertion point. With BAT and E, slotting E after the B is the only split that makes a word — BEAT.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Coast". The SHORE is the coast where land meets sea.
analyses.device: This is a container clue. "SHOE holding R" inserts the letter R into SHOE.
steps: Place R after SHO: SHO(R)E spells SHORE (5).
analyses.note: Here R lands near the end rather than the start, so test more than one gap. SHO + R + E is the split that produces the real word matching "coast".

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Dog's cry" (a bark) and "tree covering" (bark). Both are BARK.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. BARK is the noise a dog makes and the outer layer of a tree.
steps: Read "Dog's cry": a dog gives a BARK.
Read "tree covering": BARK covers a tree trunk.
analyses.note: Double definitions often pair an everyday sense with a more concrete one. The two meanings of BARK are unrelated in origin, which is exactly what makes the clue satisfying.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Close tightly" (to seal) and "sea mammal" (a seal). Both are SEAL.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. To SEAL is to fasten shut; a SEAL is also a marine animal.
steps: Read "Close tightly": to SEAL an envelope.
Read "sea mammal": a SEAL on the rocks.
analyses.note: Verb-then-noun double definitions are very common. Try reading the first sense as an action and the second as a thing — SEAL switches comfortably between the two.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Contest" (a match) and "pair up" (to match). Both give MATCH.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. A MATCH is a contest, and to MATCH is to pair things together.
analyses.note: Ignore the third meaning (a match you strike) — it is a decoy your mind may offer. The clue only needs the two senses it actually gives: contest and pair up.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Alphabet character" (a letter) and "posted message" (a letter). Both are LETTER.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. A LETTER is a symbol like A or B, and also a written message sent by post.
steps: Read "posted message": a LETTER in the mail.
analyses.note: Same spelling, two everyday meanings — the hallmark of a double definition. The (6) enumeration rules out shorter candidates and confirms LETTER.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Association" (a club) and "heavy stick" (a club). Both are CLUB.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. A CLUB is a society you join and also a blunt weapon.
analyses.note: The two senses sit far apart in meaning, which is the fun of it. With only four letters and two clear definitions, CLUB is quickly confirmed.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Heavenly being" (an angel) and "startup investor" (an angel investor). Both are ANGEL.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. ANGEL is a celestial figure and, in finance, an early backer of a company.
steps: Read "Heavenly being": an ANGEL with wings.
Read "startup investor": an ANGEL funds a new venture.
analyses.note: The modern "investor" sense is the harder half. Double definitions often lean on a specialist meaning — keep a mental list of words that have picked up business or tech senses.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Praise" (to credit someone) and "trust for later payment" (credit). Both are CREDIT.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. To CREDIT is to acknowledge or praise; CREDIT is also buying now and paying later.
steps: Read "Praise": we CREDIT her with the idea.
Read "trust for later payment": bought on CREDIT.
analyses.note: Both senses share a root (giving someone their due), so they feel related — a softer double definition than pairs like CLUB. The (6) length seals it.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Supporter" and "close companion". Both describe a FRIEND.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. A FRIEND supports you and is also someone you are close to.
steps: Read "Supporter": a FRIEND backs you up.
analyses.note: When two definitions are near-synonyms, the clue is gentle but still needs a single word that fits both naturally — FRIEND does, in six letters.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Hear". To LISTEN is to hear attentively.
analyses.device: This is an anagram, signalled by "rearranged", working on the fodder SILENT.
steps: Take the fodder: SILENT (S, I, L, E, N, T).
"rearranged" tells you to reorder the six letters.
analyses.note: This is the mirror of puzzle #2 — SILENT and LISTEN swap roles as fodder and answer. Recognising recurring anagram pairs speeds up future solves.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Shape". A TRIANGLE is a three-sided shape.
analyses.device: This is an anagram of INTEGRAL, signalled by "mixed". Both words share the same eight letters.
steps: Take the fodder: INTEGRAL (I, N, T, E, G, R, A, L).
analyses.note: Longer fodder makes the anagram harder to see at a glance. Counting letters (8) and checking they match between INTEGRAL and TRIANGLE is the reliable way to confirm.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Maker". A CREATOR is one who makes or creates.
analyses.device: This is an anagram. The indicator "reorganized" acts on the fodder REACTOR.
steps: Take the fodder: REACTOR (R, E, A, C, T, O, R).
analyses.note: REACTOR and CREATOR share all seven letters, including the two R's. With repeated letters, double-check that the counts match — two R's in, two R's out.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Flight hub". An AIRPORT is where flights depart and arrive.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are given: AIR + PORT.
analyses.note: A "port" is a place ships arrive, so AIR + PORT neatly evokes an air-travel hub. The wordplay and the definition reinforce each other.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Arc of colours". A RAINBOW is an arc of colour in the sky.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The clue gives the parts: RAIN + BOW.
analyses.note: Both parts hint at the answer — rain and a bow-shaped arc. The only cryptic step is joining them in the stated order to total seven letters.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Morning meal". BREAKFAST is the first meal of the day.
analyses.device: This is a charade with the parts supplied: BREAK + FAST.
analyses.note: There is a hidden logic — breakfast literally breaks the overnight fast. Charades often reward you with that kind of etymological wink once the parts click.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Dawn". DAYBREAK is the first light of morning.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are given outright: DAY + BREAK.
analyses.note: "Break" appears as a part here and in #39, but the answers differ entirely — proof that the surrounding piece, not the shared word, decides the solution.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Editorial office". A NEWSROOM is where news is produced.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The clue names the parts: NEWS + ROOM.
analyses.note: Compound-word charades like this are the friendliest kind: the answer is just the two named pieces written as one. Confirm with the (8) enumeration.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Support". A BRACKET is a support fixed to a wall.
analyses.device: This is a container clue. "BET holding RACK" places RACK inside BET.
steps: Split BET and insert RACK: B + RACK + ET spells BRACKET (7).
analyses.note: Here the inserted piece is a whole word (RACK), not a single letter. The container shell BET breaks after B and resumes with ET, wrapping RACK in the middle.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Neckwear". A SCARF is worn around the neck.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are SCAR + F.
analyses.note: Single-letter charades just tack a letter onto a word. SCAR plus a trailing F gives the neckwear — short, but it still rewards spotting the SCAR inside the answer.

analyses.definition: The definition is "World". A PLANET is a world orbiting a star.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are PLANE + T.
analyses.note: Watch how PLANE (an aircraft, as in #22) becomes part of a different answer here. The same string is reused across clue types — context decides its role.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Vapour". STEAM is the vapour from boiling water.
analyses.device: This is an anagram of MEATS, signalled by "cooked".
steps: Take the fodder: MEATS (M, E, A, T, S).
"cooked" tells you to rearrange the five letters.
analyses.note: "cooked" is a tasty anagram indicator that fits the surface (cooking meats). Many anagram cues are verbs of disturbance — cooked, mixed, scrambled, twisted, altered.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Flash". A SPARK is a flash of light or electricity.
analyses.device: This is a charade. "with S in front" puts the letter S before the word PARK.
steps: "S in front" adds S at the start.
analyses.note: "in front" fixes S at the beginning. Compare with #5 (TREAD), where a letter also led the word — the position word is what tells you front versus back.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Spy" (a mole) and "burrowing animal" (a mole). Both are MOLE.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. A MOLE is a secret agent planted inside an organisation, and also a small digging mammal.
steps: Read "Spy": a MOLE inside the agency.
Read "burrowing animal": a MOLE in the garden.
analyses.note: The spy sense actually grew out of the animal one — a hidden burrower. Double definitions like this feel clever precisely because the meanings are quietly linked.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Machine for lifting" (a crane) and "tall bird" (a crane). Both are CRANE.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. A CRANE lifts heavy loads on a building site, and is also a long-legged wading bird.
steps: Read "Machine for lifting": the CRANE on site.
Read "tall bird": a CRANE by the water.
analyses.note: The machine was named after the bird's long neck. Spotting that the two senses share a shape (tall, reaching) is a nice confirmation you have the right word.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Observe" (to watch) and "timepiece" (a watch). Both give WATCH.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. To WATCH is to observe; a WATCH is worn on the wrist.
analyses.note: A clean verb/noun double definition. When the first word is an action and the second is an object, look for a single word that does both jobs.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Fruit" (a date) and "appointment day" (a date). Both are DATE.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. A DATE is a sweet fruit and also a planned meeting or calendar day.
analyses.note: Four letters, two very different senses — quick to solve once you stop expecting wordplay. "or" is your signal that two plain definitions are in play.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Wordy". Something VERBOSE uses too many words.
analyses.device: This is an anagram, flagged by "scrambled", working on the fodder OBSERVE.
steps: Take the fodder: OBSERVE (O, B, S, E, R, V, E).
analyses.note: OBSERVE and VERBOSE share two E's; with repeated letters, confirm the counts match. The definition "wordy" is unrelated to observing, so trust the anagram, not the surface.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Changed". ALTERED means modified or changed.
analyses.device: This is an anagram. The indicator "upset" acts on the fodder RELATED.
steps: Take the fodder: RELATED (R, E, L, A, T, E, D).
"upset" tells you to rearrange the seven letters.
analyses.note: Notice the clue is almost self-describing: "altered" is both the answer and what anagrams do. The actual indicator is "upset" — don't mistake the definition for the cue.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Fraud". A CHEATER commits fraud or deception.
analyses.device: This is an anagram of TEACHER, signalled by "in confusion".
steps: Take the fodder: TEACHER (T, E, A, C, H, E, R).
analyses.note: There is a sly surface joke — turning a TEACHER into a CHEATER. Both have two E's, so match the letter counts to be sure the anagram is exact.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Accounts" — stories or reports. STORIES are accounts of events.
analyses.device: This is an anagram. The indicator "turns wild" works on the fodder RIOTERS.
steps: Take the fodder: RIOTERS (R, I, O, T, E, R, S).
analyses.note: "turns wild" suits the surface (rioters running wild) while signalling the anagram. RIOTERS and STORIES both carry two R's — check the counts to confirm.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Recover". To REGAIN is to get something back.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are given: RE + GAIN.
analyses.note: The prefix RE- (again) plus GAIN literally builds the meaning "gain again" — recover. Short leading particles like RE, IN or UP are common charade pieces.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Writing pad". A NOTEPAD is a pad of paper for notes.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The clue names the parts: NOTE + PAD.
analyses.note: Both pieces describe the object, so the surface and the build agree. Confirm the join with the (7) enumeration and you are done.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Carrier". An AIRLINE is a company that carries passengers by air.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are AIR + LINE.
analyses.note: AIR shows up in several charades (AIRMAIL, AIRPORT, AIRLINE). The partner word is what changes the answer — here LINE, in the sense of a transport line.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Plant". A SUNFLOWER is a tall flowering plant.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The clue gives the parts: SUN + FLOWER.
analyses.note: The name even describes the plant that turns toward the sun. When a compound word is also its own description, the charade almost solves itself.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Sea creature". A STARFISH is a star-shaped marine animal.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are STAR + FISH.
analyses.note: STAR is a frequent charade piece (see STARLIGHT, STARBOARD). Pair it with the right partner — here FISH — and check the total against the (8) enumeration.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Shore border". A COASTLINE is the outline of a coast.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The clue names the parts: COAST + LINE.
analyses.note: LINE is doing charade duty again (as in AIRLINE, HEADLINE). The leading word sets the meaning; LINE just completes the compound.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Reference mark". A FOOTNOTE is a note at the foot of a page.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are FOOT + NOTE.
analyses.note: The build mirrors the meaning — a note at the foot. NOTE also appeared in NOTEPAD (#56); the partner word, FOOT, gives this one its sense.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Night glow". MOONLIGHT is the light of the moon at night.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The clue supplies the parts: MOON + LIGHT.
analyses.note: MOON anchors a small family of charades (MOONLIT, MOONBEAM, MOONRISE, MOONLIGHT). Read the second part carefully — it is what distinguishes them.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Begin". To START is to begin.
analyses.device: This is a charade. "TART follows S" places TART after the letter S.
steps: "TART follows S" puts TART after it.
analyses.note: "follows" sets the order: the thing that follows comes second. So S leads and TART trails — S + TART, not TART + S.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Gaze". To STARE is to gaze fixedly.
analyses.device: This is an anagram of TEARS, signalled by "mixed".
steps: Take the fodder: TEARS (T, E, A, R, S).
analyses.note: TEARS, STARE, RATES and TARES are all anagrams of one another. The definition "gaze" is what selects STARE from that family.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Frighten". To SCARE is to frighten.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are S + CARE.
analyses.note: A single leading letter plus a word. Note CARE reappears as the answer in #85 — the same string plays different roles depending on the clue.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Bleak". STARK means bare, bleak or harsh.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are STAR + K.
analyses.note: STAR plus a trailing K. Compare with the STAR + word charades (#59, #81) — here the add-on is just a single letter, giving a shorter answer.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Student" (a pupil) and "center of an eye" (the pupil). Both are PUPIL.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. A PUPIL is a learner, and also the dark opening at the centre of the eye.
steps: Read "center of an eye": the PUPIL widens in the dark.
analyses.note: Both senses trace back to a word for a small thing — including the tiny reflection seen in someone's eye. A neat link hiding behind an everyday word.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Flying mammal" (a bat) and "strike" (to bat). Both give BAT.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. A BAT is a nocturnal flying mammal, and to BAT is to hit, as in cricket or baseball.
steps: Read "Flying mammal": a BAT at dusk.
analyses.note: Just three letters, so the (3) enumeration alone nearly gives it away. BAT was also a container shell in #24 — the same letters, a different job.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Tie" (a drawn game) and "sketch" (to draw). Both are DRAW.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. A DRAW is a tied result; to DRAW is to make a sketch.
steps: Read "Tie": the match ended in a DRAW.
analyses.note: A noun sense (a tie) beside a verb sense (to sketch). When the two definitions belong to different parts of speech, that contrast is itself a hint they are a double definition.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Correct" (right) and "entitlement" (a right). Both give RIGHT.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. RIGHT means correct, and a RIGHT is something you are entitled to.
analyses.note: Both senses share the idea of what is proper or due. The (5) enumeration and the two clean definitions confirm RIGHT without any letter-level work.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Box". A CRATE is a wooden box for shipping goods.
analyses.device: This is an anagram of REACT, signalled by "mixed".
steps: Take the fodder: REACT (R, E, A, C, T).
analyses.note: This reverses #8, where CRATE was the fodder and REACT the answer. The same five-letter set keeps recurring — REACT, CRATE, CATER, TRACE — so the definition is decisive.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Resin". RESIN is a sticky substance from plants.
analyses.device: This is an anagram. The indicator "mixed" works on the fodder RINSE.
steps: Take the fodder: RINSE (R, I, N, S, E).
analyses.note: RINSE and RESIN use the same five letters. A near-miss like this — where the answer looks almost like the fodder — is a quick sign you have the anagram right.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Provide food". To CATER is to provide food for an event.
analyses.device: This is an anagram of CRATE, signalled by "mixed".
steps: Take the fodder: CRATE (C, R, A, T, E).
analyses.note: Same letters as #8 and #71 again — REACT, CRATE, CATER all live in one anagram family. "Provide food" is the tag that singles out CATER this time.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Service member". An AIRMAN serves in an air force.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are AIR + MAN.
analyses.note: Another AIR-led charade. Lining up the AIR family (AIRMAIL, AIRPORT, AIRLINE, AIRMAN) shows how one common piece supports many answers.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Store for readers". A BOOKSHOP sells books.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The clue names the parts: BOOK + SHOP.
analyses.note: A straightforward compound charade — the two named words written as one. The (8) enumeration is the only check you need.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Title line". A HEADLINE is the title at the top of a news story.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are HEAD + LINE.
analyses.note: HEAD (top) + LINE neatly describes a line at the head of a page. LINE is a recurring partner — the leading word is what gives each answer its meaning.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Coastal area". The SEASIDE is the area beside the sea.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The clue gives the parts: SEA + SIDE.
analyses.note: Both pieces describe the place — the side by the sea. When a charade's parts also define the answer, you get confirmation for free.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Night ray". A MOONBEAM is a ray of moonlight.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are MOON + BEAM.
analyses.note: Another member of the MOON family. The partner word BEAM (a ray) sets this answer apart from MOONLIGHT, MOONLIT and MOONRISE.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Greeting". A HANDSHAKE is a greeting made by clasping hands.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The clue names the parts: HAND + SHAKE.
analyses.note: The build describes the action — shaking hands. HAND also appears in HANDOUT (#14); pairing it with SHAKE produces this greeting.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Emergency support". A LIFELINE is something that provides vital help.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are LIFE + LINE.
analyses.note: LINE closes out yet another charade. The metaphor — a line that saves a life — matches the definition "emergency support" exactly.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Night glow". STARLIGHT is the light given by the stars.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The clue supplies the parts: STAR + LIGHT.
analyses.note: Compare with MOONLIGHT (#62): same LIGHT ending, different source. The first part — STAR versus MOON — is what changes the answer.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Entrance mat". A DOORMAT lies at a doorway for wiping feet.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are DOOR + MAT.
analyses.note: A literal compound — a mat at the door. The two named pieces written together give the answer, confirmed by the (7) enumeration.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Drinking vessel". A TEACUP is a cup for drinking tea.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The clue names the parts: TEA + CUP.
analyses.note: TEA leads a small family (TEACUP, TEAHOUSE). The partner word — CUP here — pins the meaning. Both pieces relate to the surface, which reads naturally.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Play area". A SANDPIT is a box of sand where children play.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are SAND + PIT.
analyses.note: A pit of sand — the parts describe the thing. Charades like this are the most beginner-friendly: no insertion, no anagram, just two named words joined.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Concern". To CARE is to feel concern.
analyses.device: This is an anagram of RACE, signalled by "mixed".
steps: Take the fodder: RACE (R, A, C, E).
analyses.note: RACE, CARE and ACRE share the same four letters. CARE also appeared as a charade part in SCARE (#65) — the same string, reused in a new role.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Gem". A PEARL is a gem formed inside an oyster.
analyses.device: This is a container clue. "PEAL holding R" inserts the letter R into PEAL.
steps: Place R before the final L: PEA(R)L spells PEARL (5).
analyses.note: PEAL and PEARL differ by a single inserted R. The container indicator "holding" tells you R is tucked inside — testing the gap before L gives the gem.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Craft" — small boats. BOATS are watercraft.
analyses.device: This is a charade. "with B in front" places the letter B before OATS.
steps: "B in front" adds B at the start.
analyses.note: "in front" fixes B at the beginning, as in SPARK (#46). "Craft" is the plural sense here (boats), matched by the plural OATS — a small consistency worth noticing.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Illumination" (light) and "not heavy" (light). Both are LIGHT.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. LIGHT is brightness, and also means low in weight.
analyses.note: LIGHT was a charade ending in #62 and #81; here it stands alone with two meanings. The same word shifts from building block to full answer depending on the clue.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Fastener" (a bolt) and "run suddenly" (to bolt). Both give BOLT.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. A BOLT is a metal fastener; to BOLT is to dash away suddenly.
analyses.note: A noun (the fastener) beside a verb (to dash). That part-of-speech contrast is a recurring tell that you are looking at a double definition rather than wordplay.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Dossier" (a file) and "rasping tool" (a file). Both are FILE.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. A FILE is a folder of documents, and also a tool for smoothing or shaping.
analyses.note: The two senses are unrelated, which is what makes the clue pleasing. Four letters and a clear "or" make FILE quick to confirm.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Bright weather" (sunshine) and "cheerful mood" (sunshine). Both are SUNSHINE.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. SUNSHINE is literal sunlight, and figuratively a happy, warm disposition.
steps: Read "Bright weather": a day of SUNSHINE.
analyses.note: The figurative sense (a cheerful person) grows naturally from the literal one. Longer double definitions like this (8 letters) reward checking that both readings feel idiomatic.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Briny liquid". SEAWATER is the salty water of the sea.
analyses.device: This is an anagram, signalled by "mixed", working on the combined fodder AWE + TEARS.
steps: Gather the fodder: AWE + TEARS = the eight letters A, W, E, T, E, A, R, S.
"mixed" tells you to rearrange them all.
analyses.note: The fodder is split across two words (AWE and TEARS) before being mixed — a step up in difficulty. Count carefully: 3 + 5 = 8 letters, matching SEAWATER, with two A's and two E's on each side.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Night ascent". MOONRISE is the rising of the moon.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The clue names the parts: MOON + RISE.
analyses.note: The last of the MOON family in this archive (with MOONLIT, MOONBEAM, MOONLIGHT). RISE — an ascent — is the partner that matches "night ascent".

analyses.definition: The definition is "Famous feature". A LANDMARK is a notable feature of a place.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The parts are LAND + MARK.
analyses.note: A mark on the land — the build echoes the meaning. Two named four-letter words joined give the eight-letter answer.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Cafe". A TEAHOUSE is a cafe serving tea.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The clue gives the parts: TEA + HOUSE.
analyses.note: TEA pairs with HOUSE here, with CUP in #83. The same lead word builds different answers — always read the second part to know which one is wanted.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Skill". A TALENT is a natural skill or ability.
analyses.device: This is an anagram of LATENT, signalled by "mixed".
steps: Take the fodder: LATENT (L, A, T, E, N, T).
analyses.note: LATENT and TALENT share all six letters, including two T's — check the counts. There's a quiet wit too: a latent gift is a hidden talent.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Meal". A REPAST is a meal.
analyses.device: This is an anagram. The indicator "mixed" works on the fodder PASTER.
steps: Take the fodder: PASTER (P, A, S, T, E, R).
analyses.note: "Repast" is a slightly old-fashioned word for a meal, so trust the wordplay even if the answer is unfamiliar. PASTER and REPAST share the same six letters.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Ship side". STARBOARD is the right-hand side of a ship.
analyses.device: This is a charade. The clue names the parts: STAR + BOARD.
analyses.note: The nautical word has nothing to do with stars — the charade just borrows the STAR string. Don't let the surface sense mislead you; follow the build.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Dish". A PLATE is a flat dish.
analyses.device: This is a container clue. "LATE holding P" places the letter P with the word LATE.
steps: Add P as the clue directs.
P leads LATE to spell PLATE (1 + 4 = 5).
analyses.note: As with GROVE (#17), the added letter settles at the front: P + LATE. Test the candidate against "dish" and the (5) enumeration to confirm the placement.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Leader" (a ruler) and "measuring tool" (a ruler). Both are RULER.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. A RULER governs a country, and is also a straight strip for measuring and drawing lines.
analyses.note: Both senses come from the idea of one who rules or sets a standard. A clean five-letter double definition — confirm with the enumeration and you are done.

analyses.definition: The definition is "an expert". A MASTER is one who has expert command of a skill.
analyses.device: This is an anagram. The indicator is "Turbulent", acting on the fodder STREAM.
steps: Take the fodder: STREAM (S, T, R, E, A, M).
"Turbulent" signals an anagram of the six letters.
analyses.note: "Turbulent STREAM" reads as a vivid image while doubling as the anagram cue — the indicator describes a disturbed river. STREAM and MASTER share the same six letters.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Fairy". A SPRITE is a small fairy or elf.
analyses.device: This is an anagram. The indicator "torn" works on the fodder STRIPE.
steps: Take the fodder: STRIPE (S, T, R, I, P, E).
"torn" tells you to rearrange the six letters.
analyses.note: "emerges from torn STRIPE" hides the mechanics in a sentence — "torn" is the operative anagram word, while "emerges from" links definition to wordplay. STRIPE and SPRITE share all six letters.

analyses.definition: The definition is "the particular" — a DETAIL is a particular point or item.
analyses.device: This is an anagram. The indicator "erratically" works on the fodder TAILED.
steps: Take the fodder: TAILED (T, A, I, L, E, D).
"erratically" signals you to rearrange the six letters.
analyses.note: "note the particular" is the definition phrase (note = pay attention to), and "TAILED erratically" is the wordplay. TAILED and DETAIL are an exact anagram pair — six letters each.

analyses.definition: The definition is "floor covering". A CARPET covers a floor.
analyses.device: This is a charade where each part is clued by a synonym, not spelled out: CAR (vehicle) + PET (animal).
analyses.note: Unlike the literal charades earlier, here you must first translate each clue word into its part — "vehicle" to CAR, "animal" to PET. "carrying" links them in order.

analyses.definition: The definition is "attractive". Someone HANDSOME is good-looking or attractive.
analyses.device: This is a charade with synonym parts: HAND (give) + SOME (a few).
steps: "Give" gives HAND (as in to hand over).
analyses.note: The dash in "Give a few - that's attractive" separates wordplay from definition. Each piece is defined, not written out: HAND for give, SOME for a few.

analyses.definition: The definition is "jewellery". An EARRING is a piece of jewellery worn on the ear.
analyses.device: This is a charade with synonym parts: EAR (listen) + RING (call).
steps: "call" gives RING (as in to ring someone).
analyses.note: "Listen to the call" cleverly clues both parts at once — EAR (listen) and RING (a phone call). The surface hides the join; translating each word reveals the build.

analyses.definition: The definition is "comfort" at the end. RELIEF is comfort or ease after pain or worry.
analyses.device: This is an anagram. The fodder is two words, REF and LIE, and "about" is the indicator.
steps: Fodder: REF + LIE (6 letters: R, E, F, L, I, E).
analyses.note: Anagram fodder can span more than one word. When a single word is too short for the enumeration, try joining it to its neighbour.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Exaggeration" at the start. A TALL TALE is an exaggerated story that is hard to believe.
analyses.device: This is a charade. "lofty" gives TALL and "account" gives TALE; the colon separates definition from wordplay.
steps: TALL + TALE = TALL TALE (4,4), an exaggeration.
analyses.note: The enumeration (4,4) tells you the answer is two words of four letters each, which narrows the search a lot. Always read the numbers before the words.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Record" and "sticky strip". To TAPE something is to record it, and tape is a sticky strip.
analyses.device: This is a double definition: two meanings of the same word with no other wordplay.
steps: "Record" — to record a show is to TAPE it.
analyses.note: "Record" could be a noun (a vinyl disc) or a verb. Here the verb sense pairs with the sticky strip to give one answer.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Consider" and "raising anchor". To WEIGH something up is to consider it, and to weigh anchor is to raise it.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. The two halves describe different senses of WEIGH.
steps: "raising anchor" — sailors WEIGH anchor before setting off.
analyses.note: The surface sounds like a captain making a decision, which ties the two meanings together neatly. Old nautical phrases are a rich source of second meanings.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Combine funds" and "swimming bath". To POOL money is to combine it, and a swimming pool is a swimming bath.
analyses.device: This is a double definition, with "for the" acting as a link between the two meanings.
analyses.note: The surface reads like a club raising money for a new pool, which joins the meanings into one story. Spot the link words and the two definitions separate cleanly.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Cut a film" and "correct copy". To EDIT is both to cut and assemble film and to correct written text.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. "or" joins two senses of the same verb.
steps: "Cut a film" — film editors EDIT footage.
analyses.note: "Copy" here is a printing word for text, not a duplicate. Newspaper vocabulary (copy, proof, lead, stop press) appears often in cryptics.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Inform on" and "a store". In British slang, to SHOP someone is to inform on them; a shop is a store.
analyses.device: This is a double definition: the verb and the noun share one spelling.
steps: "Inform on" — to SHOP someone to the police.
analyses.note: The surface sounds like reporting a shop to the authorities. Slang meanings (shop, grass, nick) are common second definitions in British cryptics.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Tilt the aircraft" and "river's edge". A plane BANKS when it tilts into a turn, and a river bank is its edge.
analyses.device: This is a double definition, with "toward the" linking the two meanings.
steps: "Tilt the aircraft" — pilots BANK to turn.
analyses.note: BANK has more meanings than most words — a lender, a slope, a row of switches, to rely on — so setters can pair it in many ways. The money sense is the obvious one, which is why the clue avoids it.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Entrance" at the start. A DOOR is an entrance.
analyses.device: This is a hidden word. "in" tells you the answer is concealed in the following words, running across "condo or".
analyses.note: The surface reads like a property listing, and "flat" finishes the picture without contributing letters. Small words like "or" are easy to skip when scanning for a hidden answer.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Distant" and "controller". REMOTE means far away, and a remote is a television controller.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. The surface reads as one phrase — a boss who manages from afar.
analyses.note: Two-word double definitions often read as a single phrase. If a short clue seems to describe one thing, try reading each word as a separate definition.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Net" and "the Net". A WEB is a net or mesh, and the Web is another name for the internet.
analyses.device: This is a double definition, with "on" linking the two meanings.
steps: "Net" — a spider's WEB is a net.
"the Net" — the internet, also called the WEB.
analyses.note: The capital N signals the internet. Setters can use capitals to change a word's meaning, but they may also capitalise a word just to mislead you.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Secure" and "a curl". To LOCK is to secure, and a lock is a curl of hair.
analyses.device: This is a double definition: one verb and one noun sharing the spelling LOCK.
analyses.note: The hairdressing surface makes "secure" sound like pinning a curl in place. LOCK also means a canal lock and a rugby position, so it is a setter's favourite.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Account" and "a beak". A BILL is an account to be paid, and a bird's beak is its bill.
analyses.device: This is a double definition, with "for" linking the two meanings.
analyses.note: "Account for" looks like a single verb meaning explain, which hides the split. Breaking a phrasal verb into its parts is a common way into a double definition.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Fold" and "line at the wicket". A CREASE is a fold, and in cricket the crease is the line marked near each wicket.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. "Fold line" looks like one phrase, but "Fold" is the first definition and "line at the wicket" the second.
steps: "Fold" — a CREASE in fabric or paper.
"line at the wicket" — the batting CREASE.
analyses.note: Cricket supplies many second meanings: CREASE, OVER, DUCK, BAIL, SLIP. Even if you don't follow the game, these terms are worth learning for cryptics.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Dark red" and "drink". WINE is a dark red colour, and wine is a drink.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. The surface reads as a description of one drink, but "Dark red" is a definition in its own right.
analyses.note: Colour names borrowed from things — WINE, CLARET, PLUM, ROSE — make tidy double definitions because the surface treats the colour as an adjective.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Train" and "bus". To COACH is to train, and a coach is a long-distance bus.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. The surface suggests two kinds of transport, but "Train" is a verb.
analyses.note: The surface plants the idea of transport so firmly that "Train" looks like a noun. Always ask whether the first word could be a verb.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Halt" and "where the bus pulls in". To STOP is to halt, and a bus stop is where the bus pulls in.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. The second definition is a descriptive phrase rather than a single word.
steps: "where the bus pulls in" — a bus STOP.
analyses.note: When a clue opens with a short command like "Halt", the rest of the clue often describes the same word in a different sense.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Thames, perhaps" at the start. The Thames is a RIVER; "perhaps" marks it as an example.
analyses.device: This is a hidden word. "seen in" tells you the answer is inside "drivers".
analyses.note: The surface pictures traffic along the Thames. Hidden words inside a single longer word are easy to miss because you read the word as a whole.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Climb" and "a set of notes". To SCALE a wall is to climb it, and a musical scale is a set of notes.
analyses.device: This is a double definition, one verb and one noun.
steps: "a set of notes" — a musical SCALE.
analyses.note: Musicians really do "climb" a scale, so the surface reads as one idea. SCALE also means a fish's plate, a weighing device and a size ratio.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Drink" at the start. BEER is a drink.
analyses.device: This is a hidden word. "kept in" tells you the answer is stored inside "bee reserve".
analyses.note: Here the hidden answer starts at the very beginning of the fodder, so most of it is in plain sight. Don't assume a hidden word must start in the middle of a word.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Assess" and "the person on the bench". To JUDGE is to assess, and a judge sits on the bench in court.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. The surface suggests sport — assessing a substitute on the bench — but the bench here is a court's.
steps: "the person on the bench" — a JUDGE in court.
analyses.note: "The bench" can be a sports bench, a workbench or the judiciary. When a clue mentions one, consider all of them before settling.

analyses.definition: The definition is "start" at the end. To BEGIN is to start.
analyses.device: This is a charade. "Plead" gives BEG and "at home" gives IN; "to" links the wordplay to the definition.
steps: "at home" — IN, as when you stay in.
analyses.note: IN for "at home" is one of the most useful pieces in cryptics. The surface pictures someone pleading to stay home, which hides the join completely.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Menace" at the start. A THREAT is a menace — something or someone likely to cause harm.
analyses.device: This is a hidden word. "seen in" tells you the answer is concealed in the letters of "smooth reattachment".
analyses.note: The answer starts at the end of one word and runs into the next, splitting TH from REAT. Long words like "reattachment" are a gift to setters because they hide so many letter strings.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Nobleman" at the start. An EARL is a British nobleman, ranking above a viscount.
analyses.device: This is a hidden word. "found in" tells you the answer sits inside "pearly".
steps: Look inside the next word: PEARLY.
analyses.note: "Pearly gates" makes the surface heavenly, and "gates" plays no part in the wordplay. Here the answer is hidden inside a single word rather than across a gap.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Rogue" at the start. A RASCAL is a rogue or mischievous person.
analyses.device: This is a hidden word. "found in" tells you to look inside "ultra scale".
analyses.note: "Model" finishes the surface (a scale model) but is not part of the hidden letters. Always check exactly where a hidden answer starts and stops.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Weapon" at the start. A PISTOL is a small firearm.
analyses.device: This is a hidden word. "concealed in" tells you the answer is inside "epistolary".
steps: Look inside EPISTOLARY (a novel told in letters).
analyses.note: An epistolary novel is written as a series of letters, which is a neat joke for a clue about hidden letters. The weapon is concealed in a single word.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Fruit" at the start. A PEAR is a fruit.
analyses.device: This is a hidden word. "some" tells you to take part of "grape arbour"; "from" links to the definition.
analyses.note: The surface names one fruit (grape) to hide another. When a clue mentions an obvious answer candidate, the real answer is often concealed right next to it.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Scorch" at the start. To CHAR something is to scorch or blacken it by burning.
analyses.device: This is a hidden word. "a bit of" tells you the answer is part of "peach arrangement".
steps: "a bit of" signals a hidden word.
analyses.note: CHAR is also a fish and an old word for tea, so it appears in many disguises. The dessert surface makes "Scorch" sound like a cooking instruction.

analyses.definition: The definition is "a cooking vessel" at the end. A POT is a cooking vessel.
analyses.device: This is a reversal. "Lid" gives TOP, and "turned over" tells you to reverse it.
analyses.note: The surface describes a lid being flipped onto a pot, so the reversal indicator reads as a kitchen action. TOP/POT is one of the classic three-letter reversals.

analyses.definition: The definition is "a deity" at the end. A GOD is a deity.
analyses.device: This is a reversal. "Dog" is "brought back" — reversed — to give the answer; "as" is a link.
analyses.note: DOG/GOD is one of the oldest reversals in puzzles. Here the fodder appears in the clue as it stands, so the only work is spotting the indicator.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Exist" at the start. To LIVE is to exist.
analyses.device: This is a reversal. "evil" is "reflected" — reversed — to give the answer; "when" is a link.
steps: "reflected" — as in a mirror, reverse it.
analyses.note: "Reflected" is a natural reversal indicator because a mirror flips what it shows. EVIL/LIVE is a pair worth remembering.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Compensation" at the start. A REWARD is something given in return or as compensation.
analyses.device: This is a reversal. "coming back" tells you to reverse "drawer"; "from the" links the parts.
analyses.note: The surface suggests money coming back out of a drawer. Six-letter reversals like DRAWER/REWARD are rare, so setters return to them again and again.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Meat" at the start. STEAK is a thick slice of meat.
analyses.device: This is a homophone. "we hear" tells you the answer sounds like "stake"; "is" links the parts.
steps: "we hear" — find a word that sounds the same.
STAKE sounds like STEAK, which is meat.
analyses.note: Here the sound-alike word appears directly in the clue, so the work is choosing the spelling that matches the definition.

analyses.definition: The definition is "to compose" at the end. To WRITE is to compose a letter, song or story.
analyses.device: This is a homophone. "Correct" gives RIGHT, and "reportedly" tells you to replace it with a word that sounds the same.
steps: RIGHT sounds like WRITE, meaning to compose.
analyses.note: RIGHT has a whole family of sound-alikes — WRITE, RITE and WRIGHT — so check the definition to pick the correct spelling.

analyses.definition: The definition is "a flower" at the end. The ROSE is a flower.
analyses.device: This is a homophone. "Lines of seats" gives ROWS, and "we hear" tells you to swap it for a sound-alike.
steps: "Lines of seats" — ROWS, rhyming with nose.
ROWS sounds like ROSE, a flower.
analyses.note: ROWS has two pronunciations: lines (rhymes with "nose") and quarrels (rhymes with "cows"). Only the first sounds like ROSE, which is why the clue specifies lines of seats.

analyses.definition: The definition is "an animal" at the end. A BEAR is a large animal.
analyses.device: This is a homophone. "reportedly" tells you the answer sounds like "Bare"; "is" links the parts.
steps: BARE sounds like BEAR, an animal.
analyses.note: BEAR is also a verb (to carry or to endure), so the definition has to say which sense is meant — here "an animal" settles it.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Bread" at the start. DOUGH is unbaked bread, and both words are also slang for money.
analyses.device: This is a homophone. "a female deer" gives DOE, and "we hear" tells you the answer sounds the same; "for" is a link.
steps: DOE sounds like DOUGH, which is bread.
analyses.note: The surface pictures someone feeding bread to a deer. "Bread" works twice over here, since bread and dough are both slang for money.

analyses.definition: The definition is "a plank" at the end. A BOARD is a flat plank of wood.
analyses.device: This is a homophone. "by the sound of" tells you the answer sounds like "Bored".
steps: "by the sound of" — find a sound-alike.
BORED sounds like BOARD, a plank.
analyses.note: The surface reads as someone bored by a plank of wood. When the sound-alike word is printed in the clue, the definition tells you which spelling to choose.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Warmth" at the start. HEAT is warmth.
analyses.device: This is a deletion. "wheat losing its head" tells you to remove the first letter of WHEAT; "from" links the parts.
analyses.note: Words that still make a real word after losing their first letter — WHEAT/HEAT, GROUND/ROUND, BEAGLE/EAGLE — are the raw material for beheadings.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Weapon" at the start. A SWORD is a bladed weapon.
analyses.device: This is a hidden word. "hidden in" tells you the answer is inside "password".
analyses.note: Compound words often hide an unexpected second word that crosses their natural split: PASS-WORD contains S-WORD. Read the letters, not the parts.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Breakfast fibre" at the start. BRAN, the outer layer of grain, is a high-fibre breakfast food.
analyses.device: This is a deletion. "label" gives BRAND, and "almost" tells you to remove its last letter.
analyses.note: "Almost", "nearly" and "mostly" usually mean remove the last letter. The cereal-box surface makes "label" feel like part of the packaging.

analyses.definition: The definition is "World" at the start. The GLOBE is the world.
analyses.device: This is a charade. "good" gives G and "part of the ear" gives LOBE; the colon separates definition from wordplay.
analyses.note: G for good is common in cryptics, as in a school grade. The surface reads as "good part of the ear", so it takes a moment to split G from LOBE.

analyses.definition: The definition is "just" at the end. FAIR means just or even-handed.
analyses.device: This is a deletion. "Holy man" gives FAKIR, and "heartless" tells you to remove its middle letter; "is" links to the definition.
steps: "Holy man" — a FAKIR is an ascetic holy man.
"heartless" — remove the middle letter of F-A-K-I-R, which is K.
analyses.note: "Heartless" removes the centre of a word, so it works neatly on odd-length words like FAKIR, which have exactly one middle letter.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Christmas decoration" at the start. TINSEL is the glittering strip used to decorate Christmas trees.
analyses.device: This is an anagram. The fodder is ENLIST and "reorganised" is the indicator; "when ... is" links the parts.
steps: Fodder: ENLIST (6 letters: E, N, L, I, S, T).
analyses.note: ENLIST, LISTEN, SILENT, INLETS and TINSEL all share the same six letters — one of the richest anagram families in English.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Naval soldier" at the start. A MARINE is a soldier serving with a navy.
analyses.device: This is an anagram. The fodder is AIRMEN and "broken" is the indicator; "from" links the parts.
steps: Fodder: AIRMEN (6 letters: A, I, R, M, E, N).
analyses.note: The surface keeps everything military, so "airmen" looks like part of the story. MARINE, AIRMEN and REMAIN are anagrams of each other.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Renter" at the start. A TENANT is someone who rents a property.
analyses.device: This is a charade. "ten" is used as it stands, "an insect" gives ANT, and "joined to" puts them side by side.
analyses.note: ANT is the cryptic setter's favourite insect, along with BEE. When a clue mentions an insect, try the three-letter options first.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Hobby" at the start. A PASTIME is a hobby.
analyses.device: This is a charade. "gone by" gives PAST, followed by I and ME, used just as they stand.
steps: "then I and me" — add I and ME.
PAST + I + ME = PASTIME, a hobby.
analyses.note: The answer is built from three pieces, two of them given literally. Splitting PASTIME as PAST-I-ME rather than PAS-TIME is the key insight.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Thin soup" at the start. BROTH is a thin soup.
analyses.device: This is a container clue. "both" is used as it stands, "resistance" gives R, and "clutching" tells you BOTH wraps around R.
steps: BOTH clutching R after the B: B + R + OTH = BROTH.
analyses.note: R for resistance is one of the most frequent single-letter abbreviations in cryptics, alongside N for new and L for learner.

analyses.definition: The definition is "Fast run" at the start. A SPRINT is a short, fast run.
analyses.device: This is a container clue. "small spar" gives SPRIT, "new" gives N, and "around" tells you SPRIT goes around N.
steps: "small spar" — a SPRIT is a small spar on a sailing boat.
SPRIT around N, before the final T: SPRI + N + T = SPRINT.
analyses.note: SPRIT is an unusual word, which is why this clue is rated hard. N for new is a standard abbreviation, as in NT for New Testament.

analyses.definition: Two definitions: "Tree" and "part of the hand". Both are PALM.
analyses.device: This is a double definition. "and" joins two separate meanings of the same word.
analyses.note: Double definitions joined by "and" are the gentlest form of the device. Harder versions drop the "and", so the two meanings run together as one phrase.
